$ <HUB>/bin/agenthub --help
[exit 0]
--- stdout
brunna's single entry point (docs/design/new-user.md 3.4). A thin dispatch layer; it does not rewrite the existing scripts.

The name is `brunna` (2026-10-29: `hub` clashed with GitHub's old hub CLI; `bin/hub` stays and forwards here). `brunna install-cli`
puts a small forwarding script in ~/.local/bin, so any coding agent's session can type `brunna …` directly and the rules
files need no local paths.

Getting started:
  brunna init [--home <instance dir>] [--owner <name>] [--timezone <tz>] [--workspace <folder>] [--modules a,b] [--yes]
           [--llm runtime|anthropic|openai|ollama|none] [--llm-model <name>] [--llm-base-url <url>] [--no-launchd] [--dry-run]
                        with no hub.json, creates the instance directory (default ~/.brunna: config/ is a git repo, data/,
                        secrets/), writes config/hub.json from hub.example.json (asks a few questions; --yes takes the defaults),
                        and last writes <hub>/.hub-home pointing there; creates the folders it needs; asks which model the
                        platform's decisions go to (= brunna llm setup); installs the scheduler and watchdog (the launchd/
                        templates; left alone when unchanged); applies the config. With a hub.json already there, leaves it alone
  brunna doctor            everything that is broken, at a glance: the platform's Python, config, logins, scheduler, watchdog,
                        background services, commit gate, and whether a newer release is out
  brunna upgrade [--to vX.Y.Z | --main] [--check] [--yes]
                        move this checkout to the newest release (or that tag, or the remote's main) and bring the machine
                        in step: Python packages, registry, config apply, scheduler, hooks, CLI, doctor. Shows the
                        changelog first; --check stops there (exit 10 = an upgrade is there). Never moves a development
                        checkout (bin/upgrade.py)
  brunna init --scheduler-only   only (re)install the scheduler and watchdog from the templates (upgrade runs it)
  brunna user-settings [--update]   the platform's own entries in your tool settings (installed by you, such as
                        the worktree hooks): which are from an earlier version; --update rewrites only those
                        (upgrade runs it)
  brunna init --questions [--answers <file>] | --answers <file>
                        for an AI agent setting brunna up in its chat (README, "Set up through your agent"): the
                        questions as JSON; then the answers applied, ending with one JSON line. Consents and keys are
                        asked of you directly (a window on your screen, a page in your browser), never taken from the file
config:
  brunna config check | plan | apply [--only <applier>,...]
                        validate the config / what would change / apply (check → apply → plan again must be empty → record)
  brunna config migrate [--check]
                        bring a setting an earlier release took and this one refuses in line, and say so (upgrade runs it)
  brunna llm setup [--llm …] [--llm-model …] [--llm-base-url …]
                        who handles the platform's decisions (nightly tidy-up, weekly report): the coding agent's own login,
                        an Anthropic / OpenAI (or compatible) API key, a local Ollama; the key is not shown and goes into the
                        secrets directory; the model is picked from the list that provider actually has (the platform does not
                        guess names)
  brunna llm set-key <provider>   write the API key of hub.json llm.providers.<provider> from stdin into the platform's
                        secrets directory (chmod 600; not read from arguments, so it stays out of the shell history)
  brunna llm health        whether each provider works (= bin/llm.py health)
  brunna modules [enable|disable <name>]
                        which optional features exist and which are on; switching changes hub.json and applies it (remember
                        to commit hub.json)
  brunna move-instance --to <instance dir> [--apply]
                        move the old layout (everything in the hub root) to an instance directory: copies only, validates the
                        new layout, writes .hub-home last (delete it to go back)
projects:
  brunna connect [<folder>] [--yes] [--remote] [--dry-run]
                        connect existing folders as projects (bin/connect.py): one repo, a monorepo, or a folder of repos
  brunna onboard …         = bin/onboard-project.sh (start a new project / connect a folder)
  brunna recover <name>    = bin/recover-project.sh (new machine / the folder is gone)
  brunna rename <old> <new>  = bin/rename-project.sh (dry-run first, then add --apply)
  brunna status [project]  = bin/overview.sh
  brunna glance [--json]   what needs you and whether the platform is healthy, in one look (bin/glance.py;
                          for status bars: the herdr mod in integrations/herdr/, iTerm2, menu-bar scripts)
  brunna runtimes [check <runtime>]   the coding agents' versions: what platform runs start, each version's
                          conformance checks, the versions sessions ran (bin/runtimes.py)
  brunna first-look <project>   a newly connected project's first STATE.md now, from its README and history
                        (bin/first-look.py; brunna connect runs it)
  brunna state history <project> | restore <project> <date|commit> [--apply]
                        a project's STATE.md over time, and bringing an earlier day's back as a new commit; the owner's
                        to-do keys stay as they are now (bin/state.py)
  brunna uninstall [--apply] [--purge]
                        take brunna off this machine (bin/uninstall.py): lists first; notes stay unless --purge
scheduling:
  brunna jobs              = schedulectl list
  brunna run <job>         = schedulectl run (run it once now)
  brunna land              after a merge of brunna: rebuild the registry index from the merged code (run by
                        merge-branch; not a session command)
owner (you; not commands for project sessions):
  brunna owner list | done/drop/already-done <key> | answer <question id> "answer"
                        = bin/owner.py: the built-in owner side (hub.json owner_side: builtin; with an assistant, list only)
for project sessions (these are what the rules files name; the permission rules allow only these, not the admin commands above):
  brunna send | inbox | show | ack | pass | done | thread | open-questions …   = the project mailbox (bin/hubbus subcommands of the
                        same name)
  brunna merge-branch …    = bin/merge-branch (the merge gate for parallel sessions)
  brunna test [--tier T] [--when M] [--force] [--rev R | --index]
                        = bin/test-runner.py: the project's declared test tiers in an exported tree, a recorded pass
                        is a hit (docs/design/test-waiting.md B4)
  brunna cap-run --cap <capability> -- <command…>   = bin/hub-run (the platform runs a program the sandbox blocks)
  brunna complete <point> [--schema F] < prompt    = bin/hub-run --complete (a model call the project declares in
                                                       its registry models:, run by the platform)
  brunna agent <name> [--schema F] < prompt         = bin/hub-run --agent (a confined agent call the project declares
                                                       in its registry agents:, run by the platform in its folder)
  brunna install-cli [--dir <folder>]   put brunna's forwarding script in <folder> (default ~/.local/bin; must be on PATH)
  brunna mcp               the platform's MCP server (stdio): any coding agent with MCP can use the mailbox and write notes
                        (= bin/mcp_server.py)
  brunna mcp config        print the snippet to register in the tool's MCP settings (the platform does not change your
                        tool's settings for you; docs/mcp.md)
  brunna --version         the platform's version: the release tag this checkout is at (git describe)

--- stderr

$ <HUB>/bin/hubbus --help
[exit 0]
--- stdout
usage: hubbus [-h]
              {send,inbox,show,ack,pass,done,hook,bridge,dispatch,thread,open-handoffs,open-questions,reconcile-questions,records,record-publish,publish,status,wake-misses} ...

brunna's event bus: an append-only event log plus read cursors; project mailboxes are its projection.

positional arguments:
  {send,inbox,show,ack,pass,done,hook,bridge,dispatch,thread,open-handoffs,open-questions,reconcile-questions,records,record-publish,publish,status,wake-misses}
    record-publish      stdin: one 0.4 record or a list; sent to owner (toward the assistant). Prints for each {id:
                        record id, event: event id or null, status}

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
--- stderr

$ <HUB>/bin/schedulectl --help
[exit 1]
--- stdout
A small tool for schedule.yaml + the launchd scheduler, so you don't have to remember launchctl syntax or hand-edit yaml.

To add a schedule, just edit schedule.yaml and add a job entry. No need for this tool or for
launchd: the next scheduler.py tick (within 15 minutes) picks it up.
This tool only does what needs a command to remember, or risks breaking the yaml by hand:
pausing/resuming a single job, and turning the whole scheduler on/off and checking its state.

Usage:
  schedulectl list                list every job and its state (enabled/paused, when it runs, command)
  schedulectl pause <name>        pause a job (its settings stay; resume brings it back)
  schedulectl resume <name>       resume a job
  schedulectl status              whether the scheduler itself (launchd) is running, and the latest runs
  schedulectl logs [name] [n]     print the last n lines of a log (default scheduler.log; with name, that job's log for today)
  schedulectl run <name>          run a job once now (like Claude Desktop's "Run now") and record it as run today, so the
                                  schedule does not run it again that day (which matters for LLM jobs). Runs through launchd
                                  in the user's desktop session: under SSH the keychain can't be read and claude is logged out.
                                  With no service manager (a container) it runs right here, in the foreground.
                                  An event job runs with no events and its cursor stays: a manual run is a test. While a
                                  tick is running a job in the foreground it waits 30 seconds, then gives up
  schedulectl events <name>       an event job's cursor and the events waiting for it (and the ones the loop chain holds
                                  back): why it didn't run, what its next run gets
  schedulectl skip <name>         move an event job's cursor to the bus head: the events waiting are dropped for good (a
                                  batch that keeps failing)
  schedulectl stop                stop the scheduler completely (launchctl bootout; schedule.yaml untouched)
  schedulectl start               start the scheduler again (launchctl bootstrap)
  schedulectl models              the model each judgment point actually uses, and where that comes from (llm.model_for
                                  and hub.json's llm section)
  schedulectl set-model <point|state|index|consolidate> <model|default>
                                  write into hub.json llm.points (default = drop the pin and go back to the group's
                                  default); state = the single-project STATE.md points, index = the cross-project index.md
                                  and the weekly report, consolidate = the cleanup pass

--- stderr
